claim: PTBP1 and PTBP2 control programs of alternative splicing during neuronal development.
source: The RNA-binding proteins PTBP1 and PTBP2 control programs of alternative splicing during neuronal development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about PTBP1 and PTBP2 function, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: PTBP2 maintains embryonic splicing patterns of many synaptic and cytoskeletal proteins during differentiation of neuronal progenitor cells (NPCs) into early neurons.
source: PTBP2 was found to maintain embryonic splicing patterns of many synaptic and cytoskeletal proteins during differentiation of neuronal progenitor cells (NPCs) into early neurons.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract referencing prior findings.

claim: PTBP1 controls a program of neuronal gene expression that includes the transcription factor Pbx1.
source: We show that PTBP1 controls a program of neuronal gene expression that includes the transcription factor Pbx1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: PTBP1 represses Pbx1 exon 7 and the expression of the neuronal Pbx1a isoform in ESCs.
source: We find that PTBP1 represses Pbx1 exon 7 and the expression of the neuronal Pbx1a isoform in ESCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of regulatory elements for Pbx1 exon 7 using CRISPR-Cas9 induces Pbx1a expression in ESCs.
source: Using CRISPR-Cas9 to delete regulatory elements for exon 7, we induce Pbx1a expression in ESCs, finding that this activates transcription of neuronal genes.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: Pbx1a expression activates transcription of neuronal genes in ESCs.
source: Using CRISPR-Cas9 to delete regulatory elements for exon 7, we induce Pbx1a expression in ESCs, finding that this activates transcription of neuronal genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data in the results.

claim: PTBP1 controls the activity of Pbx1 to suppress its neuronal transcriptional program prior to induction of NPC development.
source: Thus, PTBP1 controls the activity of Pbx1 to suppress its neuronal transcriptional program prior to induction of NPC development.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Alternative splicing produces many new mRNAs encoding protein isoforms with different structures and functions that are specific to neurons.
source: In the mammalian nervous system, large scale changes in splice site choice produce many new mRNAs encoding protein isoforms with different structures and functions that are specific to neurons (Li et al., 2007; Licatalosi and Darnell, 2006; Norris and Calarco, 2012a; Raj and Blencowe, 2015a; Yap and Makeyev, 2013; Zheng and Black, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Splicing patterns are regulated in a temporal and cell-specific manner by the expression of specialized pre-mRNA binding proteins (RBPs).
source: These splicing patterns are regulated in a temporal and cell-specific manner by the expression of specialized pre-mRNA binding proteins (RBPs) (Black, 2003; Braunschweig et al., 2013; Fu and Ares, 2014; Lee and Rio, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Several RBPs have been shown to control the expression of isoforms essential for neuronal development and maturation.
source: Several RBPs have been shown to control the expression of isoforms essential for neuronal development and maturation (Charizanis et al., 2012; Gehman et al., 2011; Gehman et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Licatalosi et al., 2012; Yano et al., 2010; Jensen et al., 2000a; Iijima et al., 2011a; Ince-Dunn et al., 2012b; Quesnel-Vallières et al., 2015b).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: PTBP1 is expressed in neuronal progenitor cells and many non-neuronal cells.
source: PTBP1 is expressed in neuronal progenitor cells and many non-neuronal cells.
evidence: This is a statement of known expression pattern supported by prior literature.

claim: Upon neuronal differentiation, PTBP1 expression is repressed allowing the induction of PTBP2 and the initiation of a neuronal splicing program.
source: Upon neuronal differentiation, PTBP1 expression is repressed allowing the induction of PTBP2 and the initiation of a neuronal splicing program that is essential for neuronal maturation and survival (Boutz et al., 2007; Li et al., 2014; Licatalosi et al., 2012; Makeyev et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2012; Gueroussov et al., 2015c).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The neuronal splicing program initiated by PTBP2 is essential for neuronal maturation and survival.
source: Upon neuronal differentiation, PTBP1 expression is repressed allowing the induction of PTBP2 and the initiation of a neuronal splicing program that is essential for neuronal maturation and survival (Boutz et al., 2007; Li et al., 2014; Licatalosi et al., 2012; Makeyev et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2012; Gueroussov et al., 2015c).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Depletion of PTBP1 from fibroblasts is sufficient to drive cells towards a neuronal phenotype.
source: It has been shown that depletion of PTBP1 from fibroblasts is sufficient to drive cells towards a neuronal phenotype (Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: As neurons mature, PTBP2 expression is eventually reduced, giving rise to an adult neuronal splicing program.
source: As neurons mature, PTBP2 expression is eventually reduced, giving rise to an adult neuronal splicing program (Li et al., 2014; Licatalosi et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Transitions in PTBP1 and PTBP2 expression define three phases of neuronal maturation each with different splicing programs.
source: Together, these transitions in PTBP1 and PTBP2 expression define three phases of neuronal maturation each with different splicing programs.
evidence: This is a synthesis statement based on the prior literature cited in the paragraph.

claim: PTBP1 and PTBP2 have very similar sequences and RNA-binding properties.
source: PTBP1 and PTBP2 are encoded on separate genes and have very similar sequences and RNA-binding properties (Markovtsov et al., 2000; Oberstrass et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PTBP1 and PTBP2 target overlapping but not identical sets of splicing events.
source: These proteins target overlapping but not identical sets of splicing events (Boutz et al., 2007; Li et al., 2014; Llorian et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Some exons are responsive to both PTBP1 and PTBP2.
source: Some exons are responsive to both proteins (Boutz et al., 2007; Li et al., 2014; Spellman et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Some exons are more sensitive to PTBP1 and shift their splicing when PTBP1 is shut off early in neuronal differentiation even though PTBP2 is present.
source: In other cases, exons are more sensitive to PTBP1 and shift their splicing when PTBP1 is shut off early in neuronal differentiation even though PTBP2 is present (Boutz et al., 2007; Makeyev et al., 2007; Markovtsov et al., 2000; Tang et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: As ESCs differentiate into MNs, PTBP1 expression declines, while PTBP2 expression is induced.
source: Similar to observations in the brain, as ESCs differentiate into MNs, PTBP1 expression declines, while PTBP2 expression is induced (Figure 1B and C) (Boutz et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 1B and C, and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Day 2 MNs express the progenitor marker Nestin.
source: By immunofluorescence, Day 2 MNs express the progenitor marker Nestin, whereas Day 5 GFP+ cells express the postmitotic MN marker HB9 and the neuronal marker TuJ1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, and data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Day 5 GFP+ cells express the postmitotic MN marker HB9 and the neuronal marker TuJ1.
source: By immunofluorescence, Day 2 MNs express the progenitor marker Nestin, whereas Day 5 GFP+ cells express the postmitotic MN marker HB9 and the neuronal marker TuJ1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, and data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GFP positive cells at Day 5 express low amounts of PTBP1 and high levels of PTBP2.
source: By western blot, these GFP positive cells express low amounts of PTBP1 and high levels of PTBP2 at Day 5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At Day 8 only trace amounts of PTBP1 are found, while PTBP2 expression remains high.
source: At Day 8 only trace amounts of PTBP1 are found, while PTBP2 expression remains high (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The switch from PTBP1 to PTBP2 expression occurs during MN differentiation.
source: These results show that the switch from PTBP1 to PTBP2 expression occurs during MN differentiation, similar to earlier observations in the developing cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the western blot data presented in the manuscript and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Both PTBP1 and PTBP2 proteins are expressed in NPC cultures.
source: By western blot, we found that both PTBP1 and PTBP2 proteins were expressed in these NPC cultures.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: As NPCs are differentiated into neurons with retinoic acid, PTBP1 protein expression is lost while PTBP2 protein is induced.
source: As these NPCs were differentiated into neurons with retinoic acid, PTBP1 protein expression was lost while PTBP2 protein was induced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: The transition in PTBP1-PTBP2 protein expression is common to both EB and monolayer culture models of in vitro neuronal development, as well as embryonic brain.
source: Nevertheless, the transition in PTBP1-PTBP2 protein expression is common to both models of in vitro neuronal development, as well as embryonic brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript and comparison to prior literature.

claim: 1201 differential splicing events were identified between ESCs and MNs using a ΔPSI cutoff of 15%.
source: Using a ΔPSI cutoff of 15%, we identified a large set of alternative splicing events that change across neuronal differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B). With these filters 1201 differential splicing events were identified between ESCs and MNs, 1218 differential events between NPCs and MNs, and 750 differential events between ESC and NPC (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: 1218 differential splicing events were identified between NPCs and MNs using a ΔPSI cutoff of 15%.
source: Using a ΔPSI cutoff of 15%, we identified a large set of alternative splicing events that change across neuronal differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B). With these filters 1201 differential splicing events were identified between ESCs and MNs, 1218 differential events between NPCs and MNs, and 750 differential events between ESC and NPC (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: 750 differential splicing events were identified between ESC and NPC using a ΔPSI cutoff of 15%.
source: Using a ΔPSI cutoff of 15%, we identified a large set of alternative splicing events that change across neuronal differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B). With these filters 1201 differential splicing events were identified between ESCs and MNs, 1218 differential events between NPCs and MNs, and 750 differential events between ESC and NPC (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Differential splicing events between NPCs and MNs are enriched in biological processes and cellular compartments relevant to neuronal differentiation such as cell projection organization, axonogenesis, and cell morphogenesis.
source: Differential splicing events between NPCs and MNs were enriched (FDR<0.05) in biological processes and cellular compartments relevant to neuronal differentiation such as cell projection organization, axonogenesis, and cell morphogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is a result from Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: PTBP1 siRNA treatment depleted the protein by 80% in ESCs and 85% in NPCs.
source: PTBP1 siRNA treatment depleted the protein by 80% (n=3) and 85% (n=2) in ESCs and NPCs respectively (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from western blot analysis shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: PTBP1 depletion induced PTBP2 protein expression by four-fold.
source: As seen previously, PTBP1 depletion induced PTBP2 protein expression by four-fold (Boutz et al., 2007; Makeyev et al., 2007; Spellman et al., 2007) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B, consistent with prior literature.

claim: 418 splicing events were altered by PTBP1 knockdown in ESCs, including 362 cassette exons, 50 alternative 5' or 3' splice sites, and 6 retained introns.
source: Using the P-value and PSI cutoffs previously described, we identified 418 splicing events altered by PTBP1 knockdown in ESCs, including 362 cassette exons, 50 alternative 5' or 3' splice sites, and 6 retained introns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: 30% of neuronal exons are regulated by PTBP1 in ESCs, including 97 neuronally activated exons that are PTBP1 repressed, and 56 neuronally skipped exons that are PTBP1 activated.
source: Applying a ΔPSI cutoff of 15% for both data sets, 30% of neuronal exons are regulated by PTBP1, including 97 neuronally activated exons that are PTBP1 repressed, and 56 neuronally skipped exons that are PTBP1 activated (indicated by red and blue data points respectively in Figure 2C, left panel; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PTBP1 depletion from NPCs altered 325 splicing events (264 cassette exons, 44 alternative 5' or 3' splice sites, and 17 retained introns).
source: PTBP1 depletion from NPCs altered 325 splicing events (264 cassette exons, 44 alternative 5' or 3' splice sites, and 17 retained introns, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 16% of neuronal exons are regulated by PTBP1 in NPCs (66 PTBP1-repressed exons increased with differentiation; 23 PTBP1-activated exons decreased with differentiation).
source: Comparing this list to the splicing changes between NPCs and Day 5 GFP+ MNs identified 16% of neuronal exons regulated by PTBP1 (66 PTBP1-repressed exons increased with differentiation; 23 PTBP1-activated exons decreased with differentiation; Figure 2D, left panel; Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PTBP1/2 double knockdown increased the number of regulated neuronal exons in NPCs to 30% (116 PTBP1/2-repressed exons increased with differentiation; 45 PTBP1/2-activated exons decreased with differentiation).
source: Interestingly, PTBP1/2 double knockdown increased the number of regulated neuronal exons to 30% (116 PTBP1/2-repressed exons increased with differentiation; 45 PTBP1/2-activated exons decreased with differentiation; Figure 2D, middle panel).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Knockdown of PTBP2 alone in NPCs had only a small effect on the splicing of neuronal exons.
source: Knockdown of PTBP2 alone in NPCs had only a small effect on the splicing of neuronal exons, indicating that PTBP2 largely regulates a subset of PTBP1 targets, with relatively few targets of its own (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and D) (Figure 2D, right panel).
evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and D and Figure 2D.

claim: PTBP2 largely regulates a subset of PTBP1 targets, with relatively few targets of its own.
source: Knockdown of PTBP2 alone in NPCs had only a small effect on the splicing of neuronal exons, indicating that PTBP2 largely regulates a subset of PTBP1 targets, with relatively few targets of its own (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and D) (Figure 2D, right panel).
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data comparing PTBP1 and PTBP2 knockdown effects.

claim: PTBP1 and PTBP2 single knockdown each only moderately increased Dlg4 exon 18 splicing (ΔPSI = 8% and 13% respectively), whereas PTBP1/2 double knockdown increased exon 18 splicing by 42%.
source: In these new data, PTBP1 and PTBP2 single knockdown each only moderately increased Dlg4 exon 18 splicing (ΔPSI = 8% and 13% respectively), whereas PTBP1/2 double knockdown increased exon 18 splicing by 42%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: PTBP target transcripts in ESCs and NPCs include both unique and overlapping splicing events (80 shared, 73 unique to ESCs, 81 unique to NPCs).
source: The PTBP target transcripts in ESCs and NPCs include both unique and overlapping splicing events (80 shared, 73 unique to ESCs, 81 unique to NPCs).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis comparing ESC and NPC data.

claim: Neuronal exons regulated by PTBP1 in ESCs showed significant enrichment (FDR = 0.04) in the cellular compartment ontology term, cell junction.
source: Neuronal exons regulated by PTBP1 in ESCs showed significant enrichment (FDR = 0.04) in the cellular compartment ontology term, cell junction.
evidence: This is a result from Gene Ontology analysis.

claim: Neuronal exons regulated by PTBP1/2 in NPCs were enriched (FDR = 0.01) in the cellular compartment ontology term, cytoskeleton.
source: Neuronal exons regulated by PTBP1/2 in NPCs were enriched (FDR = 0.01) in the cellular compartment ontology term, cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a result from Gene Ontology analysis.

claim: 918,725 and 914,084 significant reads of RNA crosslinked to PTBP1 were obtained in ESCs and NPCs respectively using an FDR cutoff of 0.01.
source: Applying an FDR cutoff of 0.01, we obtained 918,725 and 914,084 significant reads of RNA crosslinked to PTBP1 in ESCs and NPCs respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from iCLIP-seq analysis.

claim: PTBP1 binding sites in both ESC and NPC were highly enriched for CU-rich pentamers.
source: As expected, PTBP1 binding sites in both ESC and NPC were highly enriched for CU-rich pentamers. The top 20 motifs included pentamers comprised of only C and U nucleotides, as well as some with G nucleotides, in agreement with the described binding specificity of PTBP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) (Amir-Ahmady et al., 2005; Han et al., 2014; Licatalosi et al., 2012; Llorian et al., 2010; Oberstrass et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a result from iCLIP-seq motif analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, consistent with prior literature.

claim: 170 PTBP1-dependent exons in ESCs are bound by PTBP1.
source: In ESCs, we identified 170 PTBP1-dependent exons that are bound by PTBP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from integrating RNA-seq and iCLIP-seq data.

claim: 108 PTBP1-dependent exons in NPCs are bound by PTBP1.
source: In NPCs, we identified 108 PTBP1-dependent exons with PTBP1 binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from integrating RNA-seq and iCLIP-seq data.

claim: A minimal set of 104 direct PTBP1 targets in ESCs and NPCs was defined, whose splicing changes during neuronal differentiation (70 Ptbp1 repressed, 34 Ptbp1 activated).
source: Overlapping all of the datasets, we defined a minimal set of 104 direct PTBP1 targets in ESCs and NPCs, whose splicing changes during neuronal differentiation (70 Ptbp1 repressed, 34 Ptbp1 activated; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from integrating multiple datasets.

claim: PTBP1 induced skipping of Gabbr1 exon 15 leads to premature translation termination in exon 16 and predicted nonsense mediated decay of the Gabbr1 mRNA.
source: PTBP1 induced skipping of Gabbr1 exon 15 leads to premature translation termination in exon 16 and predicted nonsense mediated decay of the Gabbr1 mRNA (Makeyev et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PTBP1 binding is observed within Gabbr1 exon 15 and upstream.
source: We observe PTBP1 binding within exon 15 and upstream, consistent with the increased exon 15 splicing observed during neuronal differentiation and after PTBP1 depletion (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by iCLIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Exon 7 in the Pbx1 transcript is conserved across mammals.
source: Exon 7 in the Pbx1 transcript is conserved across mammals and its inclusion leads to production of the Pbx1a isoform.
evidence: This is a statement about sequence conservation that can be verified through comparative genomics.

claim: Inclusion of Pbx1 exon 7 leads to production of the Pbx1a isoform.
source: Exon 7 in the Pbx1 transcript is conserved across mammals and its inclusion leads to production of the Pbx1a isoform.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between exon inclusion and isoform production.

claim: Skipping Pbx1 exon 7 shifts the translational reading frame to introduce a new termination codon (PTC) in exon 8.
source: Skipping exon 7 shifts the translational reading frame to introduce a new termination codon (PTC) in exon 8 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the schematic in Figure 4A and is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The translation stop in Pbx1 exon 8 does not result in NMD but instead generates the shorter isoform, Pbx1b.
source: This translation stop does not result in NMD but instead generates the shorter isoform, Pbx1b, which retains the DNA binding homeodomain but lacks the 83 amino acids at the C-terminus of Pbx1a.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional consequence of the alternative splicing event.

claim: Pbx1b retains the DNA binding homeodomain but lacks the 83 amino acids at the C-terminus of Pbx1a.
source: This translation stop does not result in NMD but instead generates the shorter isoform, Pbx1b, which retains the DNA binding homeodomain but lacks the 83 amino acids at the C-terminus of Pbx1a.
evidence: This is a statement about the structural difference between the two isoforms.

claim: During development, early embryonic tissues predominantly express Pbx1b, whereas Pbx1a is found in neural tissues.
source: During development, early embryonic tissues predominantly express Pbx1b, whereas Pbx1a is found in neural tissues (Redmond et al., 1996; Schnabel et al., 2001b).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ESCs express low levels of Pbx1b.
source: We found a similar isoform switch in cultured cells, where ESCs express low levels of Pbx1b.
evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq and RT-PCR analysis.

claim: As ESCs differentiate into NPCs and HB9+ MNs, both overall Pbx1 expression and exon 7 splicing are induced, such that MNs predominantly express the Pbx1a isoform.
source: As ESCs differentiate into NPCs and HB9+ MNs, both overall Pbx1 expression and exon 7 splicing are induced, such that MNs predominantly express the Pbx1a isoform (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The Pbx1a and Pbx1b isoforms have different transcriptional activities and cellular functions.
source: Previous work indicates that the Pbx1a and Pbx1b isoforms have different transcriptional activities and cellular functions.
evidence: This is a statement summarizing prior literature.

claim: Pbx1a and Pbx1b differ in their ability to activate or repress reporter gene expression, their interactions with the transcriptional corepressors NCoR1 and NCoR2, and their activity for cell transformation when fused to E2A.
source: The proteins differ in their ability to activate or repress reporter gene expression, their interactions with the transcriptional corepressors NCoR1 and NCoR2, and their activity for cell transformation when fused to E2A (Kamps et al., 1991; Di Rocco et al., 1997; Asahara et al., 1999b).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pbx1 exon 7 is regulated by PTBP1.
source: We find that Pbx1 exon 7 is regulated by PTBP1.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated by multiple experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Pbx1 exon 7 is derepressed as ESCs differentiate into NPCs and further into motor neurons.
source: Exon 7 is derepressed as ESCs differentiate into NPCs and further into motor neurons (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Depletion of PTBP1 from ESCs or NPCs strongly induces Pbx1 exon 7 splicing.
source: Depletion of PTBP1 from ESCs or NPCs strongly induces exon 7 splicing (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: A PTBP1 iCLIP cluster is found in the intron upstream of Pbx1 exon 7 in NPCs.
source: In NPCs, a PTBP1 iCLIP cluster is found in the intron upstream of exon 7 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by iCLIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PTBP1 iCLIP tags are not seen in ESCs presumably due to lower Pbx1 transcript levels in these cells.
source: These iCLIP tags are not seen in ESCs presumably due to lower Pbx1 transcript levels in these cells (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the iCLIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: One consequence of PTBP1 depletion during neuronal differentiation is to switch Pbx1 expression from the Pbx1b isoform to Pbx1a.
source: These data indicate that one consequence of PTBP1 depletion during neuronal differentiation is to switch Pbx1 expression from the Pbx1b isoform to Pbx1a.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Intron 6 upstream of Pbx1 exon 7 contains a PTBP1 iCLIP cluster as well as regions of mammalian sequence conservation.
source: Intron 6 upstream of exon 7 contains a PTBP1 iCLIP cluster as well as regions of mammalian sequence conservation, possibly indicative of additional splicing regulatory elements.
evidence: This is demonstrated by iCLIP-seq data and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: No homozygous deletions of the large intron 6 region (guides 1 and 4) were identified among 60 ESC clones.
source: Using guides g1 and g4, we identified no homozygous deletions among 60 ESC clones, although heterozygotes were readily isolated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is a result from CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing experiments.

claim: Clones carrying the heterozygous Intron 6 g1-g4 deletion (I6 +/-) exhibited dramatically increased exon 7 splicing.
source: Clones carrying the heterozygous Intron 6 g1-g4 deletion (I6 +/-) exhibited dramatically increased exon 7 splicing (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Exon 7 was included in only 16% of the Pbx1 mRNA in clones of the parental ESC line, whereas exon 7 was included in 51% of the mRNA in the I6 +/- clones.
source: Exon 7 was included in only 16% of the Pbx1 mRNA in clones of the parental ESC line, whereas exon 7 was included in 51% of the mRNA in the I6 +/- clones.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RT-PCR analysis.

claim: Intron 6 contains splicing silencer elements for Pbx1 exon 7.
source: This indicates that RNA from the mutant allele is almost entirely splicing in exon 7 and confirms that intron 6 contains splicing silencer elements for this exon.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CRISPR deletion experiments.

claim: The inability to isolate cells carrying homozygous mutations that increase exon 7 splicing suggests that either the gain of Pbx1a or the loss of Pbx1b is deleterious for ESC growth.
source: The inability to isolate cells carrying homozygous mutations that increase exon 7 splicing suggests that either the gain of Pbx1a or the loss of Pbx1b is deleterious for ESC growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure to isolate homozygous deletion clones.

claim: At Day 2, the I6 +/- cells predominantly expressed the Pbx1a mRNA isoform, leading to dramatically increased Pbx1a protein compared to wildtype cells.
source: At Day 2, the I6 +/- cells predominantly expressed the Pbx1a mRNA isoform, leading to dramatically increased Pbx1a protein compared to wildtype cells (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: 33 differentially expressed genes were identified in the I6 +/- cultures using a twofold change in FPKM as the cutoff (31 induced, 2 repressed).
source: Using a twofold change in FPKM as the cutoff, we identified 33 differentially expressed genes in the I6 +/- cultures (31 induced, 2 repressed).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Of the 20 transcripts that are most altered in I6 +/-, 14 are also induced as wildtype ESCs differentiate in NPCs and MNs.
source: Of the 20 transcripts that are most altered in I6 +/-, 14 are also induced as wildtype ESCs differentiate in NPCs and MNs (Figure 6—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq analysis comparing different datasets.

claim: Multiple genes induced in I6 +/- are known to play important roles in neuronal differentiation including Phox2b, Cntn2, Ntng2, Olig1, Isl1, Nrp2, Ngfr, Nav2, and Slit1.
source: Multiple genes of this group are known to play important roles in neuronal differentiation including Phox2b, Cntn2, Ntng2, Olig1, Isl1, Nrp2, Ngfr, Nav2, and Slit1 (Figure 6B), and many were previously shown to be affected by Pbx1 (Igf2, Isl1, Dlk1, and Meox1) (Kim et al., 2002; Jürgens et al., 2009b; Thiaville et al., 2012d).
evidence: This is a statement combining RNA-seq results with prior literature.

claim: Phox2b exhibited the largest change in expression in I6 +/- cells.
source: Notably, the gene exhibiting the largest change in expression was Phox2b, a marker of hindbrain visceral motor neurons and a known Pbx1a target (Pattyn et al., 2000c; Samad, 2004).
evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Phox2b is a marker of hindbrain visceral motor neurons and a known Pbx1a target.
source: Notably, the gene exhibiting the largest change in expression was Phox2b, a marker of hindbrain visceral motor neurons and a known Pbx1a target (Pattyn et al., 2000c; Samad, 2004).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 196 genes were induced and 25 genes were repressed in the I6 +/- mutant relative to the wild type cells using a 1.5-fold change in expression cutoff.
source: To increase the number of differentially expressed genes, we relaxed the cutoff to a 1.5-fold change in expression and identified 196 induced and 25 repressed genes in the mutant relative to the wild type cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Of the 196 induced genes in I6 +/-, 139 increase expression with ESC neuronal differentiation.
source: Of the 196 induced genes, 139 increase expression with ESC neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq analysis comparing different datasets.

claim: The induced genes in I6 +/- include the MN markers Olig2, Lhx3, and Mnx1.
source: Notably, the induced genes include the MN markers Olig2, Lhx3, and Mnx1 (Figure 6—source data 1), again indicating that Pbx1a is activating a neuronal transcriptional program.
evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 52 genes induced in I6 +/- have nearby Pbx1 binding sites.
source: Overlapping the 196 induced events with a published Pbx1 ChIP data set identified 52 genes with nearby Pbx1 binding (Penkov et al., 2013b) (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from integrating RNA-seq data with published ChIP-seq data.

claim: 26.5% of induced transcripts in D2 MNs exhibit Pbx1 binding, compared to 14.8% of all expressed genes, constituting a significant enrichment (p=1.06e-5).
source: Even though these binding events were identified in E11.5 embryos, 26.5% of induced transcripts in D2 MNs exhibit Pbx1 binding. This is compared to 14.8% of all expressed genes, constituting a significant enrichment of Pbx1 binding sites adjacent to induced transcripts (p=1.06e-5 by hypergeometric test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from integrating RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: All genes tested (Hoxc5, Hoxa3, Midn, Tshz3, Zfp503, and Igf1r) showed higher Pbx1 binding than an IgG control in ChIP-qPCR experiments.
source: All the genes tested, including Hoxc5, Hoxa3, Midn, Tshz3, Zfp503, and Igf1r showed higher Pbx1 binding than an IgG control, although the significance relative to the control varied (n=3, Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: There was a significant increase in Meis1 binding at the Hoxc5 locus when Pbx1a was induced in I6+/-.
source: Notably, there was a significant increase in Meis1 binding at the Hoxc5 locus when Pbx1a was induced in I6+/- (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Pbx1a may increase Hoxc5 expression through enhanced recruitment of Meis1.
source: Thus, Pbx1a may increase Hoxc5 expression through enhanced recruitment of Meis1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ChIP-qPCR data showing increased Meis1 binding at Hoxc5.

claim: Switching to Pbx1a increases the expression of genes affecting neuronal fate, including Hoxc5.
source: Together the data indicate that switching to Pbx1a increases the expression of genes affecting neuronal fate, including Hoxc5.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq and ChIP-qPCR data presented.

claim: One function of PTBP1 is to repress the neuronal form of Pbx1 and prevent its action at target genes early in development.
source: Thus, one function of PTBP1 is to repress the neuronal form of Pbx1 and prevent its action at target genes early in development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.
